items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that the residue class of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n,] denoted [MATH: [a]_n,] is the set of integers that are congruent to [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n.]

Content:
[MATH: [a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \, \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- The residue class of [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 2] corresponds to the even integers because all even integers have a remainder of [MATH: 0] when divided by [MATH: 2.]
[MATH: [0]_{2} = {0, ± 2, ± 4, …}]
- On the other hand, the residue class of [MATH: 1] modulo [MATH: 2] corresponds to the odd integers because all odd integers have a remainder of [MATH: 1] when divided by [MATH: 2.]
[MATH: [1]_{2} = {± 1, ± 3, ± 5, …}]

Content:
Notice that the residue classes [MATH: [0]_2] and [MATH: [1]_2] partition the integers, meaning that any integer belongs either to [MATH: [0]_2] or [MATH: [1]_2,] but never both.

items.readable_text:
Content:
A residue class is a particular type of a more general object called an equivalence class.

Content:
Given an equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on a set [MATH: A,] the equivalence class of an element [MATH: a \in A,] denoted [MATH: [a],] consists of all the elements of [MATH: A] that are equivalent to [MATH: a.]

Content:
[MATH: [a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, x \sim a \}]

Content:
Since any equivalence relation is symmetric, we can also write

Content:
[MATH: [a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, a \sim x \}.]

Content:
For example, consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] defined by [MATH: a \sim b] if and only if [MATH: |a|=|b|.]

Content:
Under this relation, two integers are equivalent if they have the same absolute value. The first few equivalence classes are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [0]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼0}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|=|0|}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|= 0}; = {0}; [1]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼1}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|=|1|}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|= 1}; = {± 1}; [2]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼2}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|=|2|}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|= 2}; = {± 2}; [3]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼3}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|=|3|}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|= 3}; = {± 3}; ⋮]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Equivalence relations can have a finite or infinite number of equivalence classes. This particular equivalence relation has an infinite number of equivalence classes.
- For equivalence classes containing more than one element, we can use any element to represent the class. For example, [MATH: [1]] and [MATH: [-1]] represent the same equivalence class.

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on [MATH: \mathbb{Z},] defined by [MATH: x \sim y] if [MATH: 12 \,|\, (x-y).] Which of the following are in the equivalence class [MATH: [9]?]

  1. [MATH: 9]

  2. [MATH: 21]

  3. [MATH: 22]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on [MATH: \mathbb{Z},] defined by [MATH: x \sim y] if [MATH: 12 \,|\, (x-y).] Which of the following are in the equivalence class [MATH: [9]?]

1. [MATH: 9]
2. [MATH: 21]
3. [MATH: 22]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The equivalence class [MATH: [9]] consists of the elements that are equivalent to [MATH: 9] under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

[MATH: [9]|= {x ∈ Z: x∼9}; = {x ∈ Z: 12|(x − 9)}; = {x ∈ Z: x = 9 + 12k, k ∈ Z}; = {…, − 15, − 3, 9, 21, 33, …}.]

We see that [MATH: 9] and [MATH: 21] are in [MATH: [9],] while [MATH: 22] is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

sections.normalized_html: The properties of residue classes generalize to equivalence classes. Let's list some of them:
sections.readable_text: The properties of residue classes generalize to equivalence classes. Let's list some of them:

sections.normalized_html:
• If [MATH: a \sim b] then [MATH: [a]=[b].] This allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.

Content:
The properties of residue classes generalize to equivalence classes. Let's list some of them:

Content:
- If [MATH: a \sim b] then [MATH: [a]=[b].] This allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.
- On the other hand, two distinct equivalence classes have an empty intersection:
[MATH: a \not\sim b
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a] \cap [b] = \emptyset]
- The residue classes form a partition of [MATH: A.] Moreover, [MATH: A] can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct equivalence classes:
[MATH: A = \bigcup_{i\in I}\,[a]_i]
where [MATH: [a]_i] denotes the [MATH: i]'th residue class and [MATH: I] is an index set spanning all possible classes.

Content:
Consider once again the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] defined by [MATH: a \sim b] if and only if [MATH: |a|=|b|.] We found that the equivalence classes were as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [0]|= {0}; [1]|= {± 1}; [2]|= {± 2}; [3]|= {± 3}; ⋮]

Content:
These equivalence classes form a partition of the set of integers:
[MATH: \big\{[0], [1], [2],\ldots\big\}]

Content:
Moreover, the integers can be constructed from the disjoint union of these classes:

Content:
[MATH: Z|= [0]∪[1]∪[2]∪⋯; = {0}∪{± 1}∪{± 2}∪⋯]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on the set [MATH: A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},] defined by [MATH: a \sim b] if [MATH: \textrm{i}^a = \textrm{i}^b,] where [MATH: \textrm{i}] is the imaginary unit in [MATH: \mathbb{C}.] How many distinct equivalence classes does [MATH: \sim] partition [MATH: A] into?
sections.readable_text: Consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on the set [MATH: A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},] defined by [MATH: a \sim b] if [MATH: \textrm{i}^a = \textrm{i}^b,] where [MATH: \textrm{i}] is the imaginary unit in [MATH: \mathbb{C}.] How many distinct equivalence classes does [MATH: \sim] partition [MATH: A] into?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The equivalence classes of [MATH: \sim] partition [MATH: A,] meaning that any element [MATH: a \in A] belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of [MATH: A] have been placed into an equivalence class.

[MATH: [0]|= {a ∈ A∣a∼0}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}^{0}}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = 1}; = {0, 4, 8}; [1]|= {a ∈ A∣a∼1}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}^{1}}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}}; = {1, 5, 9}; [2]|= {a ∈ A∣a∼2}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}^{2}}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = − 1}; = {2, 6}; [3]|= {a ∈ A∣a∼3}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}^{3}}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = − \textrm{i}}; = {3, 7}]

Each element of [MATH: A] has been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have [MATH: 4] distinct equivalence classes:

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that the residue class of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n,] denoted [MATH: [a]_n,] is the set of integers that are congruent to [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n.]

Content:
[MATH: [a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \, \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- The residue class of [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 2] corresponds to the even integers because all even integers have a remainder of [MATH: 0] when divided by [MATH: 2.]
[MATH: [0]_{2} = {0, ± 2, ± 4, …}]
- On the other hand, the residue class of [MATH: 1] modulo [MATH: 2] corresponds to the odd integers because all odd integers have a remainder of [MATH: 1] when divided by [MATH: 2.]
[MATH: [1]_{2} = {± 1, ± 3, ± 5, …}]

Content:
Notice that the residue classes [MATH: [0]_2] and [MATH: [1]_2] partition the integers, meaning that any integer belongs either to [MATH: [0]_2] or [MATH: [1]_2,] but never both.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2f64e034833908f141d8fff951fdae86]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Equivalence Classes

Content:
A residue class is a particular type of a more general object called an equivalence class.

Content:
Given an equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on a set [MATH: A,] the equivalence class of an element [MATH: a \in A,] denoted [MATH: [a],] consists of all the elements of [MATH: A] that are equivalent to [MATH: a.]

Content:
[MATH: [a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, x \sim a \}]

Content:
Since any equivalence relation is symmetric, we can also write

Content:
[MATH: [a] = \{ x \in A \, | \, a \sim x \}.]

Content:
For example, consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] defined by [MATH: a \sim b] if and only if [MATH: |a|=|b|.]

Content:
Under this relation, two integers are equivalent if they have the same absolute value. The first few equivalence classes are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [0]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼0}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|=|0|}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|= 0}; = {0}; [1]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼1}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|=|1|}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|= 1}; = {± 1}; [2]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼2}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|=|2|}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|= 2}; = {± 2}; [3]|= {a ∈ Z∣a∼3}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|=|3|}; = {a ∈ Z∣|a|= 3}; = {± 3}; ⋮]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Equivalence relations can have a finite or infinite number of equivalence classes. This particular equivalence relation has an infinite number of equivalence classes.
- For equivalence classes containing more than one element, we can use any element to represent the class. For example, [MATH: [1]] and [MATH: [-1]] represent the same equivalence class.

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Elements Belonging to an Equivalence Class

Example Prompt:
Consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on [MATH: \mathbb{Z},] defined by [MATH: x \sim y] if [MATH: 12 \,|\, (x-y).] Which of the following are in the equivalence class [MATH: [9]?]

1. [MATH: 9]
2. [MATH: 21]
3. [MATH: 22]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The equivalence class [MATH: [9]] consists of the elements that are equivalent to [MATH: 9] under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

[MATH: [9]|= {x ∈ Z: x∼9}; = {x ∈ Z: 12|(x − 9)}; = {x ∈ Z: x = 9 + 12k, k ∈ Z}; = {…, − 15, − 3, 9, 21, 33, …}.]

We see that [MATH: 9] and [MATH: 21] are in [MATH: [9],] while [MATH: 22] is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Equivalence Classes Containing a Given Element

Example Prompt:
Consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on [MATH: \mathbb{R},] defined by [MATH: x \sim y] if [MATH: \sin x = \sin y.] Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2}?]

1. [MATH: \left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]]
2. [MATH: \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]]
3. [MATH: \left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \in [x]] if [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \sim x.] Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

[MATH: \sin ((π)/(2))|= \sin x; 1|= \sin x; \sin x|= 1.]

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \not\in \left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]] because [MATH: \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) =-1\neq 1 \quad \color{red}\times]
- [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \not\in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]] because [MATH: \sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) =-1\neq 1 \quad \color{red}\times]
- [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \in \left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]] because [MATH: \sin \left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 1 \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

Item 9 — Tutorial: Properties of Equivalence Classes

Content:
The properties of residue classes generalize to equivalence classes. Let's list some of them:

Content:
- If [MATH: a \sim b] then [MATH: [a]=[b].] This allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.
- On the other hand, two distinct equivalence classes have an empty intersection:
[MATH: a \not\sim b
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a] \cap [b] = \emptyset]
- The residue classes form a partition of [MATH: A.] Moreover, [MATH: A] can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct equivalence classes:
[MATH: A = \bigcup_{i\in I}\,[a]_i]
where [MATH: [a]_i] denotes the [MATH: i]'th residue class and [MATH: I] is an index set spanning all possible classes.

Content:
Consider once again the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] defined by [MATH: a \sim b] if and only if [MATH: |a|=|b|.] We found that the equivalence classes were as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [0]|= {0}; [1]|= {± 1}; [2]|= {± 2}; [3]|= {± 3}; ⋮]

Content:
These equivalence classes form a partition of the set of integers:
[MATH: \big\{[0], [1], [2],\ldots\big\}]

Content:
Moreover, the integers can be constructed from the disjoint union of these classes:

Content:
[MATH: Z|= [0]∪[1]∪[2]∪⋯; = {0}∪{± 1}∪{± 2}∪⋯]

---

Item 10 — Example: Counting Equivalence Classes

Example Prompt:
Consider the equivalence relation [MATH: \sim] on the set [MATH: A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},] defined by [MATH: a \sim b] if [MATH: \textrm{i}^a = \textrm{i}^b,] where [MATH: \textrm{i}] is the imaginary unit in [MATH: \mathbb{C}.] How many distinct equivalence classes does [MATH: \sim] partition [MATH: A] into?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The equivalence classes of [MATH: \sim] partition [MATH: A,] meaning that any element [MATH: a \in A] belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of [MATH: A] have been placed into an equivalence class.

[MATH: [0]|= {a ∈ A∣a∼0}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}^{0}}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = 1}; = {0, 4, 8}; [1]|= {a ∈ A∣a∼1}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}^{1}}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}}; = {1, 5, 9}; [2]|= {a ∈ A∣a∼2}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}^{2}}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = − 1}; = {2, 6}; [3]|= {a ∈ A∣a∼3}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = \textrm{i}^{3}}; = {a ∈ A∣\textrm{i}^{a} = − \textrm{i}}; = {3, 7}]

Each element of [MATH: A] has been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have [MATH: 4] distinct equivalence classes:

[MATH: [0] = \{ 0, 4, 8 \} , \quad [1] = \{ 1, 5, 9 \}, \quad [2] = \{ 2, 6 \}, \quad [3] = \{ 3, 7 \}.]
